title: Turn octopus, spaghetti, and more of your favorite foods into crackers with Senbei Maker 2
description: You haven’t truly eaten a food until you’ve made it into a cracker. Who doesn’t love a good cracker? They’re dry, portable, can be customized with a vast range of toppings, or be used as toppings themselves. But the current range of commercially available crackers could be better. It seems the cracker industry is largely […]
content:
You haven’t truly eaten a food until you’ve made it into a cracker.

Who doesn’t love a good cracker? They’re dry, portable, can be customized with a vast range of toppings, or be used as toppings themselves. But the current range of commercially available crackers could be better. It seems the cracker industry is largely hung up on cheese and salt for the most part.

But Japan’s premier random appliance maker Thanko has come out with a product that can unleash the full potential of crackers by allowing us to create flavors limited only by the human imagination. The machine is called Senbei Maker 2, wherein “senbei” is the Japanese word for cracker, although a senbei is typically thicker and harder than some conventional crackers like saltines.

The machine harnesses the patented technique of making any food of your choice into a cracker by heating it up and squeezing it really hard. The following video shows it in action, creating crackers out of French fries, melon pan, spaghetti, and whitebait.

With a little ingenuity, there’s no limit to what you can transform into a cracker. Note that while certain, highly mushable foods like french fries will naturally unify upon crackerification, some might need a little help. For example, in the video, a little batter is added to help the white bait stick together, and cheese can also make a sturdy and flavorful matrix.

▼ It’s easy as one, two, three.

Difficult-to-squish foods like walnuts or jawbreakers should also be avoided or pre-crushed into a finer crumb or powder so they don’t damage the machine. But other than that, you’re pretty much free to make crackers out of whatever you want. In fact, Thanko even suggests going ahead and tossing a whole octopus in there.

There’s no better feeling than being able to compress all your favorite dishes, whether it’s duck a l’orange or wasps, into edible discs that you can carry around in a file folder. Just don’t put a cracker in the cracker makers. That’s a paradox that might make reality collapse in on itself.

Senbei Maker 2 sells for around 5,500 yen (US$35) at various online retailers, including Thanko’s own website. It’s not clear what improvements were made on the original Senbei Maker for this model, making it kind of like the Evil Dead 2 of cracker makers, in which it’s hard to tell whether this is a true sequel or a reboot.

And also like Evil Dead 2, it doesn’t really matter, because its just a whole lot of gooey fun, so what are you waiting for? Pick one up and get crackering.

Source, images: PR Times

title: Nephew of Studio Ghibli director Hayao Miyazaki serves up Totoro Shaved Ice in Tokyo
description: Find out if these limited-edition sweets uphold the family reputation for quality and creativity. If you’re a Studio Ghibli fan in Japan, one place you should definitely put on your list of places to visit is Shirohige’s Cream Puff Factory. Currently owned and run by the nephew of Ghibli director Hayao Miyazaki, Shirohige’s has two […]
content:
Find out if these limited-edition sweets uphold the family reputation for quality and creativity.

If you’re a Studio Ghibli fan in Japan, one place you should definitely put on your list of places to visit is Shirohige’s Cream Puff Factory. Currently owned and run by the nephew of Ghibli director Hayao Miyazaki, Shirohige’s has two stores in Tokyo – one in Kichijoji and one in Daita near Shimokitazawa – but the main Daita location is where fans are flocking to right now, because it’s the only place in Japan where you can get Totoro Shaved Ice.

▼ Only available for a very limited time, there are three varieties to choose from: Strawberry, Peach, and Matcha, priced at 2,000 yen (US$12.58) each.

We headed to the store to try the new desserts, and when we arrived at about 10:00 a.m., roughly half an hour before opening, there were already around 30 people in line ahead of us. It was a hot day, but staff showed a great deal of care for everyone outside, providing customers with cups of cold water and tea. Hayao Miyazaki’s younger brother, who ran the shop with his wife for many years before recently handing over the reins to son Yosuke, was also present, kindly handing out mosquito repellent to everyone in line, so the wait to enter the store didn’t seem too long at all.

▼ We placed our order inside, above the store’s signature Totoro cream puffs…

▼ …and were given two cards for our order – one peach and one matcha.

Artistic talent clearly runs in the Miyazaki family, as the menu and cards were beautifully illustrated. Creative touches can be seen throughout the store, and even outside, where the banner marked with the kanji for “ice”, commonly hung outside stores that sell shaved ice desserts in Japan, had been personally embellished.

This sweet message, penned and drawn by Miyazaki’s brother, shows the Catbus from My Neighbour Totoro being carried by Spirited Away’s Yu-Bird in fly form. Alongside it is the traditional summer greeting “暑中お見舞い申し上げます” (“shochu omimai moshiagemasu”), which expresses well wishes for the hottest time of year.

After admiring all the little details, it didn’t take long for staff to call out our order numbers and hand over our delectable-looking Totoros, which looked even cuter in real-life than they did in the pictures.

Starting with the peach version, which also happens to be the staff favourite, we were immediately impressed by the freshness of the white peaches and the beautiful hue of the syrup, which is made by simmering nectarines and plums.

Each shaved ice dessert comes with a beautiful white Small Totoro on the side, which is designed to sit between the larger Totoro’s ears, on a mint leaf.

▼ The Small Totoro is made using the same traditional nerikiri technique used to create moulded wagashi sweets.

It almost seemed a shame to interfere with such a work of art, but things were beginning to melt fast under the sunlight.

With the larger Totoro’s ears starting to disappear, the big eyes of the Small Totoro seemed to widen, as if imploring us to hurry up and eat it.

▼ Grabbing the spoon, we took a chunk out of Totoro’s stomach.

The ice was firm yet crumbly, creating just the right amount of texture to keep the structure sturdy and upright, giving us enough time to enjoy the accompanying ingredients.

▼ The peach was delicious – perfectly ripe with a fruity, refreshing sweetness.

The ice cream had a very pronounced taste of vanilla, as if it had been homemade, adding a lovely touch of richness to the sweetness of the peach.

▼ The bite-sized kanten pieces glistened in the dappled sunlight.

Kanten is a traditional type of agar, made from red seaweed, which is commonly used to make firm jellies and desserts in Japan.

▼ These were firm and smooth, with just the right amount of bite to help carry the flavour of the syrup.

The syrup really is the star of the show here, imparting a sweet-yet-tart fruity accent to the entire dessert. You could tell it had been carefully prepared, with the slow simmering process creating the perfect balance between flavours, and with just the right amount to take you through to the very last mouthful.

▼ Feeling refreshed from the fruity iced dessert, we were now keen to try the matcha variety.

This Totoro is surrounded by the same ingredients you’d see in anmitsu, a popular traditional Japanese dessert.

Setting it apart from other desserts, however, is the Totoro factor, with the large Totoro adding extra coolness to the already refreshing combination of ingredients.

▼ The mini Totoro wagashi adds a subtle sweetness and chewiness to the mix.

It’s the matcha that steals the show, though, with both the ice cream and syrup made with a generous amount of fragrant Uji matcha.

▼ The syrup pairs well with the anko bean paste, which retains a lot of the beans to give it a lovely coarse texture.

It’s also a good match for the kanten in the dessert, which consists of both plain and matcha varieties, adding greater depth and richness to match the bold flavours.

▼ Shiratama dumplings add another textural accent, and taste particularly good with a generous serving of matcha syrup.

Even when combined with the shaved ice, this remains a very rich dessert, filled with luscious, traditional flavours.

▼ Though the icy treat looked cute to start with…

▼ …it somehow remained cute right to the end, as the mini Totoro took a tumble and wound up looking as if it was swimming in matcha.

The Totoro in our peach dessert also dove into the syrup and ended up losing an eyeball, but still managed to look cute all the same.

Both desserts were absolutely delicious, and although we weren’t able to try the third flavour, strawberry, judging by the cries of delight from people who tried it nearby, it was just as good as these two.

Made with quality ingredients, the attention to detail in these desserts reflects the quality you’d expect from a place that bears the Miyazaki name.

The Totoro Shaved Ice is one of the cutest and best-tasting desserts you’ll find in Japan at the moment, but it won’t be around for long. Available on just six days, 21-23 and 28-30 August, the shaved ice is only being made in limited quantities so be sure to get there early to avoid missing out.

Cafe information
Shirohige’s Cream Puff Factory / 白髭（しろひげ）のシュークリーム工房
Address: Tokyo-to, Setagaya-ku, Daita 5-3-1
東京都世田谷区代田５-３-１
Open 10:30 a.m.-6 p.m., closed Tue ( or Wed if Tue is a public holiday)

title: Winnie the Pooh cosplays as Yuzuru Hanyu for new plushie collaboration
description: Apparently it’s not a bother at all for Pooh Bear to dress up like the Japanese skating star. Yuzuru Hanyu’s fondness for Winnie the Pooh is well known, and the Japanese figure skating legend’s fanbase has created a tradition of showering the ice with plushies of the character after his performances. But is Pooh Bear […]
content:
Apparently it’s not a bother at all for Pooh Bear to dress up like the Japanese skating star.

Yuzuru Hanyu’s fondness for Winnie the Pooh is well known, and the Japanese figure skating legend’s fanbase has created a tradition of showering the ice with plushies of the character after his performances. But is Pooh Bear himself one of Hanyu’s fans?

That might seem like an impossible question to answer, given that Winnie the Pooh, like most fictional animated characters, isn’t in the habit of giving interviews. But as they say, actions speak louder than words, and so it’s probably safe to say that Pooh likes Hanyu too, since he’s now cosplaying as the skater.

Publisher Kodansha is getting set to release To Pooh-san: Yuzuru Hanyu and Pooh-san Memory Book. The 40-page book contains a photo collection and exclusive interview with Hanyu, and to sweeten the deal, it comes bundled with a 20.5-centimeter (8.1-inch) tall Winnie the Pooh plushie. For this collaboration, Pooh is forgoing his customary red polo shirt and instead going with more fantastic fashions.

The plushie comes with two outfits, recreating the costumes worn by Hanyu at the 2018 Pyeongchang Winter Olympics, where he won the second of his gold medals. The ensemble Pooh is wearing in the above image is the same as the one Hanyu wore for his free-skate program to the musical piece titled “Seimei.”

And if you change Pooh into his alternate included set of clothes, he’ll match what Hanyu was wearing for his short program skate to Chopin’s “Ballade No. 1.”

Also part of the package are a 51.5 x 72.8-centimeter poster and reproduction of a handwritten note that Yuzuru penned to Pooh.

Kodansha is asking 22,000 yen (US$138) for To Pooh-san: Yuzuru Hanyu and Pooh-san Memory Book and its bundled merch, and all units are being produced to order. On the one hand, that means that pre-ordering is required, but it also means that actual fans are guaranteed to be able to purchase the set without having to go through a scalper.

▼ Yuzuru posing with Pooh dressing as Yuzuru…honestly, this does seem like a missed opportunity for the skater to have worn the bear’s shirt.

Pre-orders are open between now and October 20 through Amazon Japan and Rakuten (here and here), with Amazon listing shipping as slated for late May of 2027. And if you need even more Yuzuru Hanyu/Winnie the Pooh crossover merch, there’s the pair’s also recently revealed Shower of Heart collection.

title: Nagoya’s famous Shinkansen platform noodle shop has other, better branches nearby
description: Travelers love Sumiyoshi’s kishimen, but there’s a way to skip the long line and get a better deal on your meal. Nagoya an outstanding destination for traveling foodies, thanks to the city’s numerous tasty claims to fame, including tempura shrimp rice balls, a special kind of local miso, and a unique breakfast culture. Then there’s […]
content:
Travelers love Sumiyoshi’s kishimen, but there’s a way to skip the long line and get a better deal on your meal.

Nagoya an outstanding destination for traveling foodies, thanks to the city’s numerous tasty claims to fame, including tempura shrimp rice balls, a special kind of local miso, and a unique breakfast culture. Then there’s Nagoya’s representative type of noodles, kishimen, broad udon noodles with a soy sauce-based broth.

Kishimen is so strongly associated with Nagoya that you can even find great places to try it inside Nagoya Station. Travelers regularly form a long line outside Sumiyoshi, a stand-and-eat kishimen joint on the Shinkansen platform.

▼ The Shinkansen platform Sumiyoshi

However, while passing through Nagoya Station the other day we found out that Sumiyoshi also has kishimen stands on three non-Shinkansen platforms, and these are the better ones to go to, for two reasons. First, they’re less crowded, or at least they were when we stopped by on a weekday afternoon. At that time, the Shinkansen platform branch, as usual, had a line to get in, but we could walk right into the Sumiyoshi on the non-Shinkansen Line 5/6 platform Sumiyoshi with no waiting.

▼ The Line 5/6 platform Sumiyoshi

The other reason to visit one of the non-Shinkansen Sumiyoshi branches? The One-coin Kishimen, which is exclusive to the regular-line branches.

▼ ワンコインきしめん = One-coin Kishimen

The “one coin” here refers to the price of just 500 yen (US$3.15), which is also the largest-denomination yen coin. Suiyoshi already charges 450 yen for a bowl of just plain kishimen noodles, and most topping options beyond some simple seaweed will cost you 700 yen or more. The One-coin Kishimen, though, is a thoroughly satisfying bargain.

Along with the noodles, you get a nicely sized tempura shrimp, some aburaage (fried tofu), katsuobushi (bonito flakes) and sliced green onion.

This isn’t a mini portion of kishimen to make up for the toppings, either. It’s a full-sized serving of noodles, with barely any additional charge for all the extras that are in the bowl with them. And the low price isn’t the result of the non-Shinkansen Sumiyoshi branches using lower-quality ingredients or skimping on seasonings either. We asked the staff if there was any difference between how the regular and Shinkansen-line locations prepare their noodles, and were informed that they all make their kishimen the exact same way.

All it took was a single taste to confirm that the staff was telling the truth. This tasted every bit as good as the Sumiyoshi kishimen we’d eaten on the Shinkansen platform on a previous visit, just at a more budget-friendly price.

In addition to the Line 5/6 platform branch that we ate at, Sumiyoshi also has kishimen stands on the Line 1/2 and 3/4 platforms, and it’s a pretty safe bet that their noodles are equally delicious. And should you be looking for dessert afterwards, Krispy Kreme Japan has some special donuts in Nagoya that you can’t get anywhere else in the world.

title: Ohaw? Ruibe? Pocche? While traveling in Japan’s north, we try Ainu cuisine for the first time
description: Taste-testing the northern frontier of local foods in Japan. Just about every corner of Japan has some special food it’s famous for, and if you head up to the country’s northern tip, Hokkaido Prefecture, there are several. Travelers often arrive in Hokkaido licking their lips as they look forward to some of the country’s best […]
content:
Taste-testing the northern frontier of local foods in Japan.

Just about every corner of Japan has some special food it’s famous for, and if you head up to the country’s northern tip, Hokkaido Prefecture, there are several. Travelers often arrive in Hokkaido licking their lips as they look forward to some of the country’s best salmon roe, sea urchin, and crab, plus delicious miso ramen, soup curry, and all sorts of cheeses and dairy desserts.

But on our recent visit to Hokkaido, the most memorable things we ate were the ones we hadn’t ever heard of before this trip: ohaw, ruibe, and pocche.

If you’re an experienced eater of Japanese cuisine yet don’t recognize any of those, don’t fell like you’ve got to turn in your foodie card. All of those dishes come from the culture of the Ainu, the indigenous people who populated Hokkaido before the arrival of Japanese settlers and the region’s absorption into Japan. Though Hokkaido’s Ainu population is far smaller than it used to be, cultural centers like Akanko Ainu Kotan, near the shore of Lake Akanko, help to preserve Ainu cultural traditions and share them with visitors.

In addition to a theater with traditional dance performances and shops selling handicrafts, Akanko Ainu Kotan also has restaurants where you can try Ainu dishes, and with our visit coming right around launch time, we decided to check out the eatery Marukibune.

▼ 丸木舟 = Marukibune

After sitting down, we opened up the menu and took a look. While such standard dishes as soy sauce broth ramen and curry rice are available, we wanted a literal taste of Ainu culture, so that’s what we gravitated towards…

…and for our first step into this new-to-us food frontier, we selected the yuk kam ohaw.

Breaking that down linguistically, ohaw is a kind of stew made with fish or other animal stock and kelp. Kam ohaw means that there’s meat in the stew, and yuk indicates that the meat here is venison.

Our ohaw also contained root vegetables and wild garlic.

It looked very different from the sort of soups common to mainstream Japanese cooking, and we braced ourselves for something that could possibly be an acquired taste. That apprehension turned out to be unnecessary though, as we found it immediately delicious.

Despite the generous portion of venison, there was no gaminess at all to the flavor profile, which was instead fortifying yet simple and comforting. It was so good that we think we might find ourselves craving a bowl of ohaw once the winter chill sets in later this year.

Next up: parimomo ruibe.

Ruibe is the Ainu equivalent to sashimi, but with a few key differences. First, ruibe is prepared, and served, frozen. Second, while conventional sashimi consists pretty much entirely of saltwater seafood, ruibe is made with freshwater fish as well. In our case, parimomo is the Ainu word for the fish called Ezo ugui in Japanese (whose scientific name is Pseudaspius sachalinensis), a relative of the freshwater minnow.

Marukibune catches its Ezo ugui from Lake Kussharoko, which isn’t too far away from the restaurant, so it’s fresh and flavorful, with a sweetness that comes to a clean finish. The mouthfeel of the frozen fish slices, and the sensation of the texture changing as they thawed as we chewed, took a little getting used to, but made for an enjoyably stimulating change of pace from regular sashimi.

We also ordered a kotandon. This is a donburi (rice bowl) topped with strips of grilled pork, wild garlic, onion, and egg, flavored with a salty sweet marinade.

To be honest, we’re not sure exactly how traditional the kotandon is. In addition to being part of Akanko Ainu Kotan’s name, kotan is the Ainu word for a village or community. It seems like the kotandon might be a more modern fusion concession to visitors to Akanko Ainu Kotan who want something that’s a nod to Ainu culture but isn’t going to feel too challenging. None of that changes the fact, though, that this is a very tasty rice bowl, and one that just about anyone will probably enjoy.

And last, we ordered a pocche set.

That might look like a plate of cookies accompanying our cup of tea, but pocche are actually preserved potatoes. Hokkaido gets very cold in winter, and pocche are traditionally made by leaving potatoes outside until they freeze, then bringing them inside to thaw, and repeating the process enough times for fermentation to take place.

So rather than a dessert, pocche were actually a way to make sure the entire potato harvest could get eaten. They have a chewy texture but no sweetness beyond that which you’d find in a regular potato. We can’t really say they tasted particularly good, but they didn’t taste bad either, and they’re an interesting way to experience hands-on one way that the Ainu culture turned the harsh conditions of Hokkaido’s winter weather into a positive.

As for prices, our ohaw was 1,200 yen (US$7.50 yen), the ruibe 1,100 yen, the kotandon (which also came with a side of ruibe) 2,600 yen, and the pocche set 1,100 yen. Taking the portion sizes into account, those prices are a little on the high side, but it was money well spent for such a unique meal.

After eating, it’s also well worth your time to take a look at the rest of Akanko Ainu Kotan too.

We especially recommend the Ikor Theater, which hosts three different traditional storytelling dance performances.

Even without a reservation, we were able to catch the Ainu Ancient Ceremonial Dance program, which presents an inaw, a ceremonial tool mean to form a connection between performers and the kamuy (Ainu gods). The dances aren’t flashy, but seated in the theater, with the light of open-flame torches illuminating the dancers and singers, we were comfortably mesmerized for the 30 minutes the performance lasts.

As an added bonus, the nearby Lake Akanko is quite beautiful too, whether you’re admiring the scenery from the shore of from the deck of one of the boats offering cruises for day trippers.

So if you’re looking to broaden not only your cultural knowledge, but also your palate, while you’re in Hokkaido, stop on by Akanko Ainu Kotan and Marukibune.

title: Narita Airport Transit & Stay Program returns after six years with free tours and festival experiences
description: Immerse yourself in a lesser-known side of Japan, minutes away from the famous international airport.  Narita City in Tokyo’s neighbouring Chiba Prefecture tends to be overlooked as a travel destination, with a lot of overseas visitors bypassing it on their way in and out of the country through Narita Airport. The area around the airport […]
content:
Immerse yourself in a lesser-known side of Japan, minutes away from the famous international airport. 

Narita City in Tokyo’s neighbouring Chiba Prefecture tends to be overlooked as a travel destination, with a lot of overseas visitors bypassing it on their way in and out of the country through Narita Airport. The area around the airport really is worth exploring, though, as it retains a traditional charm with historic shrines and temples, a famous Edo-style traditional shopping street, and lots of special workshops and experiences for tourists.

To help visitors explore these charms, Narita Airport is bringing back its special free guided tours, which were introduced in 2015 but suspended due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Designed for transit passengers and foreign tourists staying around the airport, the “Narita Airport Transit & Stay Program” will officially restart on 1 October, after a six-year absence, with English-speaking volunteer guides providing free tours and an additional paid “Plus” series, for special experiences that reveal a deeper side of the area.

There are six free guided tours:

▼ Narita City (3-hour tour)

This tour takes you to Naritasan Shinshoji, a temple with 1,000 years of history, and the Omotesando shopping street, where you can pick up souvenirs and snacks at traditional stores.

▼ Naritasan Shinshoji is 25 minutes by train from Narita Airport.

▼ Katori City (5-hour tour)

Here you’ll find a riverside town with a beautiful traditional atmosphere, where you can take part in Sawara Hariko, a traditional paper-mache craft local to the area.

▼ Katori is 41 minutes by train from Narita Airport.

▼ Tako (4-hour tour)

Famous for its rice, this town boasts a beautiful green landscape and rural scenery, which you can easily explore by renting an electric-assist bicycle.

▼ Tako is 23 minutes by train from Narita Airport.

▼ Shibayama (4-hour tour)

Two of the highlights on this tour are a visit to the Museum of Aeronautical Sciences and a home-style buffet lunch, with a wide variety of local ingredients, on weekdays.

▼ Shibayama is 26 minutes by train from Narita Airport.

▼ Sakae (5-hour tour)

Slip into a yukata and step back in time at a beautiful open-air museum called Boso no Mura (“Boso Village”).

▼ Sakae is 27 minutes by train from Narita Airport

▼ Kozaki (6-hour tour)

Dubbed the “village of fermentation”, this part of Chiba prides itself on brewed and fermented products, with two sake breweries in the area, as well as miso stores and bakeries that use natural yeast made from sake lees (a byproduct of the sake-making process).

A visit to Kozaki Shrine is another highlight of the tour, and it’s said to be a good place for travelers to pray for safe journeys as it’s home to the guardian deity of aviation, transportation, and industry.

▼ Kozaki is roughly 31 minutes by train from Narita Airport.

Though the guided tours are free, participants need to cover their own expenses such as transportation, meals and admission fees. As for the paid Transit & Stay Program, there are currently nine to choose from, including a one-hour brewery tour and tasting for 1,000 yen (US$6.31)…

▼ … a knife-forging experience (4 hours, from 32,800 yen)…

…and entry to the World Boshuriken Tournament, where you can dress in a ninja costume and try out some ninja techniques for yourself (5.5 hours, 23,800 yen).

▼ What’s likely to really draw tourists, though, is the chance to participate in a local festival.

Pulling a festival float is usually only reserved for people who live in the neighbourhoods where the festival is being held, so this is a rare opportunity to immerse yourself in the culture and rub shoulders with the locals.

The first festival-focused tour to be offered is the Otaiyasai Festival on 5 September, which is being treated as a pre-official launch event. Taking around five hours and priced from 15,800 yen, this tour takes place at the Sogo Reido temple, which is half an hour by train from the airport.

Those pressed for time can enjoy a shorter two-hour float-pulling experience at the Narita Gion Festival on Omotesando Street from 8-11 July 2027…

… while those wanting maximum festival immersion can stay overnight during the Narita Gion Festival, with the float-pulling experience followed by time in a special viewing room at the Waqoo Naritasan Monzen hotel.

One night’s accommodation at Waqoo Naritasan Monzen with breakfast and dinner are also included in the deal, all for 84,000 yen.

These tours prove that the area around Narita Airport really is home to some great hidden gems. So if you’re passing through the region, or looking for something to do during a long layover, these Transit & Stay tours are a great way to explore outside the airport and experience a lesser-known side of Japan with the help of a local.

Reservations for the free tours open on 15 September and can be made here, while the paid tours are available to purchase now from this site.

title: Japan’s double-decker portable rice cooker/bento maker is better than ever with new version
description: Now there’s even more to be thankful to Thanko for. Japanese gadget maker Thanko has repeatedly shown its knack for innovations to be grateful for, but the company’s best idea of all is arguably its One-Person Rice Cooker Series. These compact kitchen appliances let you cook enough rice for a single serving, and their easy […]
content:
Now there’s even more to be thankful to Thanko for.

Japanese gadget maker Thanko has repeatedly shown its knack for innovations to be grateful for, but the company’s best idea of all is arguably its One-Person Rice Cooker Series. These compact kitchen appliances let you cook enough rice for a single serving, and their easy portability means that you can take them with you and cook your rice at your office desk or wherever else you need to be in the early part of the day, letting you enjoy freshly steamed rice once your lunch break comes around.

Of course, even Japanese people don’t eat just rice for lunch, so Thanko also makes two-tier one-person rice cookers. The bottom section is for cooking the rice, and the steam that rises from it is channeled into the upper section stacked on top of it, where it can cook, reheat, or thaw whatever vegetables, dumplings, curry roux, or other side dishes that you’re pairing with your rice.

With restaurant prices rising, Thanko says it’s seeing even higher demand than usual for its one-person rice cookers, and so the company’s designers have made a few improvements. First, they’ve managed to make the cooking process even speedier, and it now takes just 14 minutes to have a batch of rice ready to eat. They’ve added a timer function that will automatically start the cooking process one, two, or three hours after you set it. This new feature was added in order to make the one-person rice cooker easier to use with brown rice, which benefits from a longer soaking period than white rice, and thus increase the variety of meals that can be made with the device.

The one-person rice cooker is even a handy option for car camping, since it’ll work with vehicle power outlets as long as they put out at a voltage of at least 300 watts.

And yes, it’s still as compact as ever and easily breaks down into its component parts for easy cleaning.

▼ The parts shown at the bottom left are even dishwasher-safe.

The new and improved double-decker one-person rice cooker is priced at 8,980 yen (US$56) and just went on sale this week through the Thanko online store here.

title: Wait, some Shinkansen trains already have private booths that only cost 1,500 yen for an hour?
description: High-speed serenity has been low-key available on the Shinkansen for a long time with hardly anyone noticing it. A new Supreme Class is coming to Shinkansen trains this fall, offering luxurious private cabins for those with deep pockets. It turns out, though, that some bullet trains in Japan have quietly had available private booths for […]
content:
High-speed serenity has been low-key available on the Shinkansen for a long time with hardly anyone noticing it.

A new Supreme Class is coming to Shinkansen trains this fall, offering luxurious private cabins for those with deep pockets. It turns out, though, that some bullet trains in Japan have quietly had available private booths for years, and at very affordable prices.

If you’re wondering how this service has managed to escape the attention of so many travelers in Japan, it’s because the private booth is only offered on certain trains, and can only be reserved by certain passengers. Specifically, it’s only found on N700S-series Nozomi Shinkansen trains running on the Tokaido and Sanyo lines (i.e. between Tokyo and Fukuoka’s Hakata Station), and the booth can only be booked by passengers who’ve also purchased a regular seat in Car 7. The booth is located in the connecting area between Cars 7 and 8, and is equipped with two chairs, a counter, standard and USB power outlets, and a window so that you can watch the scenery zoom by from your private space.

You can use the booth either by yourself or with one other traveling companion, and rather than booking it for the length of your trip, it can be reserved, in 10-minute increments, for a block of time up to two hours.

So what’s the surcharge, on top of your Car 7 regular class Shinkansen ticket, to use this private booth? Hardly anything. Prices are just 200 yen (US$1.25) per 10 minutes up to a half-hour, and 300 yen per 10 minutes between 30 and 60 minutes, which works out to 600 yen for a 30-minute session or 1,500 yen for a full hour (payment is done by credit card). Things get a little pricier after that, with 90 minutes costing 2,500 yen and two hours 4,000 yen, but still, this a pretty affordable pocket of serene solitude.

Another likely reason this booth has largely escaped attention from travel fans is that, despite being available since 2022, it hasn’t been pitched to luxury travelers. In fact, JR calls it the Business Booth, and its exclusive availability to Car 7 on N700S Nozomi trains is because Car 7 is designated as the S Work car, which is promoted as being a car for passengers who need to get some work done during their ride. As such, the Business Booth isn’t outfitted with swanky interior fittings, and was primarily designed as a place where you can open up your laptop, lay out some documents, and make phone calls or hold video conferences with professional colleagues. All that said, it still remains a place you can have all to yourself for a while during your Shinkansen journey, even if all you want to do is relax.

Use of the Business Booth cannot be reserved ahead of time. Instead, after boarding you can check for/claim available time blocks via a QR code displayed at the booth’s entrance or on a pamphlet at your seat.

And, once again, the Business Booth is exclusive to N700S Nozomi trains, and if you’re looking for one, JR Central allows you to check which Shinkansen of that class are running on the current day by clicking on the button labeled ビジネスブースを搭載している今日の列車はこちら on their official website here.

Source: JR Central via Maidona News

title: KFC Japan unveils new Tsukimi collection that takes moon-viewing to extreme levels
description: Eggs run wild for this ever-evolving Japanese tradition. As we head towards autumn in Japan, the change of seasons brings with it one of the country’s most famous seasonal events: Tsukimi, or “Moon Viewing”. Traditionally, Tsukimi, which takes place on 25 September this year, involves seasonal foods like round dango rice dumplings, which people enjoy […]
content:
Eggs run wild for this ever-evolving Japanese tradition.

As we head towards autumn in Japan, the change of seasons brings with it one of the country’s most famous seasonal events: Tsukimi, or “Moon Viewing”. Traditionally, Tsukimi, which takes place on 25 September this year, involves seasonal foods like round dango rice dumplings, which people enjoy while gazing at the moon. With modern lifestyles these days, though, the tradition has evolved somewhat, with fast food chains now adding limited-edition Tsukimi items to the menu, usually featuring a fried egg, due to the way the egg resembles the full moon.

One of the collections we look forward to most every year is the “Torori Tsukimi” series (“torori” means “melty”) from KFC Japan. This year the chain is going all out with the moon-viewing, giving us five limited-edition menu items, three of which are marked as new, with four containing a fried-egg-style omelette filled with a rich and melty egg-yolk sauce.

▼ “新” means “New”

Starting with the more familiar items, which are so popular they’ve become something of a standard release every year, we have the Torori Tsukimi Filet Burger (590 yen [US$3.95]) and the Torori Tsukimi Twister (490 yen), both of which get an eggy upgrade.

▼ The Twister adds teriyaki sauce and mayonnaise for even more melty enjoyment.

The two new burgers take things a step further, with “Kobore Tartar” (“kobore” means “spilling out”) and wafu katsu (“Japanese-style cutlet”) being key ingredients in addition to the egg.

▼ Torori Tsukimi Wafu Katsu Burger Kobore Tartar (640 yen)

▼ Torori Triple Tsukimi Wafu Katsu Burger Kobore Tartar (990 yen)

This towering burger stacks three eggs on top of each other, creating what KFC describes as “an egg-filled burger with plenty of visual impact”. Though the chain bills this as a new release, it was available at seven KFC locations last year (we know because our own reporter Mr Sato tried it). Due to glowing reviews, the chain decided to roll it out at all its branches around Japan this year, so more people can enjoy the triple tower of moon-viewing enjoyment.

▼ Rounding out the collection is the Omochi to Noko (“rich”) Custard no Tsukimi Pie (320 yen, or 450 yen for two)

The dessert also gets an eggier upgrade to qualify as a new release this year, with 20 percent more custard filling compared to its last appearance. The custard is made with Madagascar vanilla beans and is paired with a chewy mochi filling, all wrapped up in crispy pie pastry.

This year’s campaign also comes with a deliciously over-the-top concept video, starring T.M.Revolution frontman Takanori Nishikawa as “T.M.G. Revolution”, with “T.M.G.” standing for “tamago” or “egg”.

The new 30-second video will be released on 26 August, alongside a commercial called “Eggs Run Wild”, starring Japanese model and television personality Shiori Sato.

KFC’s new Tsukimi collection proves you can never have too much egg during moon-viewing season, and it’ll be available while stocks last from 26 August.

title: The Japanese government is ending its Cool Japan Fund program
description: Cool Japan’s mission has been accomplished, but not because of Cool Japan. Back in 2013, the Japanese government’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry had an idea. What if they created a program to promote the appealing aspects of Japanese culture, including pop culture, to people around the world? This wasn’t going to be a […]
content:
Cool Japan’s mission has been accomplished, but not because of Cool Japan.

Back in 2013, the Japanese government’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry had an idea. What if they created a program to promote the appealing aspects of Japanese culture, including pop culture, to people around the world? This wasn’t going to be a stuffy, overly academic way of looking at Japanese culture, either, but rather a way of spreading the word about all the ways Japan is cool.

And thus was born the Cool Japan Fund, which describes itself as “a public-private fund with the aim of contributing to the sustainable growth of Japan’s economy through the expansion of overseas demand and supply of attractive products and services unique to Japanese lifestyle and culture.” Entertainment content such as anime, manga, and pop music were among the areas to be championed, along with food, fashion, technology, and tourism attractions.

With the rapid rise in global enthusiasm for Japanese stuff over the last decade and a half, one might expect the Cool Japan Fund to have been a huge success, but that’s actually not the case at all. Instead, in 2025 the Cool Japan Fund’s deficit grew to a staggering 54 billion yen (US$340 million), and now the Japanese government is ready to effectively shut the program down.

Inside sources have leaked to multiple media organizations that the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry’s upcoming 2027 budget proposal will not be asking for any funds for the Cool Japan Fund. This would remove the program’s ability to invest in any new projects, and since investing is pretty much all the Cool Japan Fund does, by extension, this would terminate the program, since the chance of the it somehow rising out of being 54 billion yen in the red while in a dormant state is negligible.

▼ We don’t know how many sofas there are in the ministry’s offices, but there probably don’t collectively contain enough dropped change to balance the Cool Japan Fund’s budget.

As for how the Cool Japan Fund got itself into such a dire situation, the program has been criticized for picking poor partners for more than a decade, with detractors saying Cool Japan was in the habit of providing vague, unhelpful support to projects with poor prospects. Among the most recent embarrassments is the Cool Japan Fund’s backing of Junglia Okinawa, a dinosaur-themed amusement park/resort that opened in Okinawa last year. Almost immediately, Junglia was mocked by Japanese travelers for its high prices and dull attractions, and foreign tourists, who were charged more for admission due to Junglia’s two-tier ticket prices, seemed even less interested in visiting.

The irony here is that while the Cool Japan Fund was flailing and floundering, Japan still managed to build a reputation as one of the coolest countries in the world. Global interest in Japanese media franchises, food, and travel has skyrocketed, just not for the specific partners that the Cool Japan Fund was pushing. Part of that recent boom is, undeniably, stems from the yen’s recent weakness making Japanese products and vacations suddenly very affordable for people from other countries, and arguably some of the Cool Japan Fund’s early swings-and-misses might have performed better had they taken place with today’s exchange rates. The bigger takeaway, though, is that Japanese businesses and private-sector organizations have shown themselves to be perfectly capable of showing the world the cool stuff they have without the Cool Japan Fund’s help.

So in an odd way, while the Cool Japan Fund itself didn’t accomplish the goal is set out to, that goal has still been accomplished. In a time when cost of living increases are making middle and lower-class Japanese households tighten their belts, it’s for the best that the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry stop throwing taxpayer money at a program whose help isn’t needed, and whose efforts probably wouldn’t be very helpful anyway.

Source: Asahi Shimbun via Yahoo! Japan News via Jin, Mainichi Shimbun, Cool Japan Fund

title: Kyoto’s Meiji-era mansion opens a private tearoom with stained glass for just one day
description: A rare East-meets-West tea ceremony in a seldom seen tearoom. A country’s culture is often deep and never-ending, always with new facets to explore, but the point where two cultures meet and blend is no less fascinating. In the case of Japan, it has led to things like the tradition of yoshoku (Western dishes adapted […]
content:
A rare East-meets-West tea ceremony in a seldom seen tearoom.

A country’s culture is often deep and never-ending, always with new facets to explore, but the point where two cultures meet and blend is no less fascinating. In the case of Japan, it has led to things like the tradition of yoshoku (Western dishes adapted for Japanese tastes), and modern musical groups like Wagakki Band, which blends rock with traditional Japanese instruments. The fusion of Japanese and Western cultures stretches into many fields, and one of these can be seen in Kyoto. Within the city, a landmark that bridges these two worlds exists as Hotel Chorakukan.

Built in 1909 during the Meiji era (1868–1912) by wealthy tobacco industrialist Kichibei Murai, Chourakukan was originally designed as a grand villa to entertain foreign diplomats, nobility, and prominent global figures. Its construction reflected an era when Japan was rapidly modernizing and actively welcoming the West, with its outer appearance utilizing a brick and stone-heavy design characteristically found in European countries rather than the more wooden structures found in traditional Japanese architecture. Over a century later, the mansion still serves as an elegant venue where traditional Japanese heritage and European luxury harmonize.

To celebrate this legacy, the hotel will host the annual Art Festival in Chourakukan 2026 on September 27. In its fifth installment, the festival aims to introduce the history, architectural beauty, and guest-receiving traditions of Chorakukan to the public. Under this year’s theme of Architecture and Hospitality Culture, the one-day event offers a variety of cultural, artistic, and culinary experiences.

While there are several activities to do at the festival, from incense making to enjoying a French dinner course, one of the main highlights of the festival is the opportunity for general visitors to attend a special Tea Serving Experience (known as “teicha”) in Chorakuan, a magnificent third-floor tearoom that is usually kept strictly private.

Teicha is the formal act of preparing matcha and entertaining guests and can be seen to be a significantly shorter and more streamlined version of a full-scale, formal tea gathering (“chaji”). A chaji could last anywhere up to four hours, following a strict sequence of events and ceremonies, and participants are expected to hold a deep knowledge of the complex etiquette involved. Teicha, on the other hand, usually lasts in the range of 30 to 45 minutes, with the host preparing matcha alongside a seasonal confection without the ritual.

The tearoom Chorakuan is built as a replica of Zangetsutei, a famous historic tearoom originating from Omotesenke, one of the three main historical schools of Japanese tea ceremony. While classical tearooms emphasize simplicity, Chorakuan features vibrant stained-glass windows depicting spring cherry blossoms and autumn foliage.

The event will be held over six sessions between 10:30 a.m. and 5:15 p.m., with each being approximately 45 minutes. These sessions will accommodate ten guests per session, and advance reservation is required, making for a very exclusive experience. Tickets cost 2,500 yen (US$16), which includes admission to the Art Festival, or if you happen to have already picked up a ticket to the festival, the tea experience will cost an additional 2,000 yen.

After September 27, the tearoom Chorakuan will once again close its doors to the public, until the next special event comes around. Enjoying matcha served alongside seasonal sweets in a traditional room illuminated by Western stained glass offers an unforgettable East-meets-West experience, so keep your eyes out for the next opportunity if you happen to miss out. Or try out other avenues of mixed cultures by rocking a denim kimono or making your own sushi burgers.

Venue: Hotel Chourakukan / 芸術祭 in CHOURAKUKAN 2026
